query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a conformal nanometric nickel coating on tungsten particles prior to composite consolidation improves interfacial bonding with the surrounding copper matrix, reducing void formation and phase separation while preserving mechanical durability under irradiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite prepared from tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions embedded in a copper matrix, as typically processed via spark‐plasma sintering or mechanical alloying.
generation.intervention: Deposit a uniform, thin (e.g., ~5 nm) Ni layer on the tungsten particles via atomic layer deposition (ALD) before mixing with copper powder and sintering.
generation.conditions: Following ALD, the Ni-coated tungsten particles are blended with copper powder and subjected to spark-plasma sintering under vacuum at temperatures around 900–1000 °C (well below Cu boiling point) with a controlled hold time to ensure full densification. Post-sintering, the composite is evaluated under simulated fusion-reactor conditions (elevated temperature, neutron/gamma irradiation, thermal cycling) in laboratory testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial nickel layer acts as a binder that promotes enhanced wetting and interdiffusion between tungsten and copper, leading to improved interparticle contact and reduced porosity at the interface.
generation.mechanism: The nickel interlayer facilitates diffusional bonding during sintering by lowering interfacial energy mismatch and enhancing atomic mobility at the tungsten–copper boundary. This promotes uniform contact and minimizes void formation and phase segregation, which are otherwise caused by the large melting/boiling point differences between W and Cu.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline composite (e.g., one produced by spark-plasma sintering of uncoated tungsten particles), the ALD Ni-coated version is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in thermal conductivity and improved mechanical durability (e.g., higher fatigue resistance and less void-related degradation) under irradiation-simulated service conditions.
generation.baseline: Sintered composites using uncoated tungsten particles in a copper matrix produced by conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying, which tend to show defects such as voids and phase separation.
generation.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective in the processing temperature range up to about 1000 °C and under service conditions typical of fusion reactor joints (e.g., thermal cycling, moderate irradiation doses). Extreme irradiation environments or conditions causing excessive interdiffusion might require separate evaluation.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the nickel interlayer under extended irradiation and high thermal cycling is not fully known; also, potential formation of brittle intermetallic compounds at the interface could counteract some benefits if processing conditions are not optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites: one using uncoated tungsten particles (baseline) and one using tungsten particles coated with a ~5 nm Ni layer via ALD. Both sets are consolidated via identical spark-plasma sintering protocols. Subsequent samples are exposed to laboratory-simulated fusion reactor conditions (e.g., thermal cycling between room temperature and 300 °C, combined with controlled neutron irradiation doses).
measurements: High-resolution microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess interfacial bonding and void formation
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., laser flash analysis) pre- and post-irradiation
Mechanical testing (e.g., fatigue or flexural strength tests) under ambient and post-irradiation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated composites do not show a statistically significant improvement in interfacial density (fewer voids), thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability compared to the baseline uncoated composites, or if they demonstrate premature brittleness due to intermetallic formation, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.
